Based on the healthcare Q&A matches, the answer to your question is that patients with a history of a prior preterm birth are at an increased risk of having recurrent preterm birth and cervical shortening in a subsequent pregnancy.

This is supported by a study that found that women who had previously given birth prematurely (PPROM or PTL) were more likely to experience recurrent preterm births compared to women whose pregnancies were not affected by prior preterm birth. The study also noted that this increased risk was associated with cervical shortening, suggesting that the underlying causes of preterm birth may still be present in subsequent pregnancies.

While the exact mechanisms behind this relationship are unclear, it is thought that the pre-existing conditions and hormonal changes that led to preterm birth may not fully resolve or change in subsequent pregnancies, increasing the likelihood of recurrence. Therefore, healthcare providers should be aware of this increased risk when counseling women on the potential for recurrent preterm birth in their subsequent pregnancy.
